newsitem.title: UK: Argos seeks exact terms of EU court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Argos seeks exact terms of EU court ruling.

text.p: Bob Stewart, finance director of retail chain Argos, said it was unclear what impact a VAT tax ruling by the European Court would have on the company.

"It seems to be good news for the company but we need to see the exact terms of the ruling," Stewart told Reuters. Earlier the European Court upheld a move by Unilever subsidiary Elida Faberge and Argos to have the UK government pay back excess value-added-tax paid on discounted goods.
"What exactly the terms of the ruling are is uncertain. We are trying to find out. For instance, does it apply specifically to gift vouchers or to promotional vouchers in general."

Argos is the UK's market leader in gift vouchers for corporate customers which constitutes slightly more than one percent of total turnover, said Stewart. Argos showed turnover of 1.52 billion stg in the 12 months to June 15, 1996.
Argos sells gift voucher to corporate clients for promotional use at a small discount. The Court said in such cases VAT was payable on the discounted and not the full price.

The court agreed that Britain's tax authorities had wrongly interpreted EU VAT rules. Argos is seeking reimbursement from the UK's Customs and Excise of some 1.363 million, while Elida Gibbs, a Unilever subsidiary, is asking for 883,894 stg.
Customs and Excise calculated the VAT payable by Argos on the basis of receipts from sales of goods, regardless of the discounted value of the vouchers used in some cases.

The action brought by Elida Gibbs involved a money-off coupon scheme in which coupons had a face value that customers could cut out from newspapers or magazines and present in partial payment for some Elida Gibbs toiletry products.
"We are very pleased with the ruling, but we need more time to assess the full implications," said a Unilever spokesman.
The company was also offering a cash-back coupon scheme, refunding consumers part of the full purchase price paid.
In a separate statement, Britain's Treasury estimated the potential cost of value added tax cases would be around 200 million stg.
The Treasury said some press reports that the ruling could cost billions of lost revenue were mistaken and the potential cost of Argos style voucher schemes alone would be just 65 million stg.
